questions.q: Why does this lesson say a design document presenting exactly one option isn't really offering a decision?
options: Because Salesforce architecture reviews require a minimum of three options by policy
Because it's effectively asking for a rubber stamp, with no way to tell if the option won on its merits or just by being the only candidate shown
Because single-option documents are always technically wrong
Because stakeholders never approve single-option proposals
questions.explain: Without a real alternative to compare against, a reviewer has no basis to judge whether the presented design actually won on its merits — it's a rubber-stamp request dressed up as a decision document.

questions.q: Which of this lesson's five tradeoff dimensions is described as the easiest to lose track of once a design becomes technically interesting?
options: Total cost
Time to value
Fit to the stated requirement
Risk and blast radius
questions.explain: Fit to the stated requirement is singled out as the dimension most at risk of getting lost — a design can become impressive on its own terms while quietly drifting away from the specific requirement the stakeholder actually asked for.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about two designs rarely dominating each other on every dimension at once?
options: It means the comparison was done incorrectly
It only happens when comparing designs across different Salesforce clouds
It means neither design should be chosen
It's the normal shape of a real tradeoff, which is why the relative importance of each dimension has to be settled before scoring either design
questions.explain: One design being faster/cheaper while another is more flexible/lower-risk is the ordinary outcome of a genuine tradeoff — which is exactly why 'which is better' can't be answered until the stakeholder's priorities among the dimensions are settled first.

questions.q: In the Ferro single-org-vs-multi-org comparison this lesson scores, what does the lighter-weight multi-org-plus-integration option trade away relative to full consolidation?
options: It doesn't fully deliver a true single combined Account record, but scores better on risk and cost since each unit's existing processes stay untouched
It fully satisfies "one combined Account record," but costs much more to maintain
It eliminates all reporting capability across units
It requires abandoning Salesforce entirely for all three units
questions.explain: The lighter integration option sacrifices some fit to the 'one Account record' requirement in exchange for meaningfully lower risk and cost, since it leaves each unit's existing processes alone rather than reconciling all three into one org.

questions.q: Which tradeoff dimension specifically asks what happens if a design turns out to be wrong, and how contained the resulting damage would be?
options: Flexibility for known future change
Risk and blast radius
Time to value
Total cost
questions.explain: Risk and blast radius is the dimension that asks about the consequences of being wrong and how far those consequences would spread — distinct from cost (what the design costs to build and run) or time to value (how soon it pays off).
